title: ByteDance sued by automotive photography firm EVOX, alleging TikTok parent copied 7,095 images to train its Seedream AI image generator
summary: Automotive photography firm EVOX sues ByteDance over 7095 images used to train Seedream AI
detailed: Automotive photography firm EVOX Productions filed a copyright infringement lawsuit against TikTok parent ByteDance in the US District Court.
The lawsuit alleges ByteDance accessed EvoxStock.com servers without authorization and copied 7,095 images to train its Seedream AI image generator.
EVOX claims it spent over 30 years and approximately $56 million building a library of over two million photographs.
This matters because it highlights growing legal conflicts between commercial content copyright holders and AI companies training generative models.
sentences: TikTok parent ByteDance is being sued for copyright infringement by automotive photography company EVOX Productions.
The lawsuit alleges that ByteDance copied 7,095 of EVOX’s photographs without permission and used them to train Seedream, ByteDance’s AI image generator.
The complaint was filed in the US District Court for the Central District of California on October 29 and can be read in full here.

According to the filing, Seedream is now generating images “so substantially similar to the EVOX images that they are now destroying the market for the originals.”
EVOX, based in Chino, California, says it has spent more than 30 years building a library of photographs covering several thousand vehicle makes and models.
The company says it owns the copyrights to more than two million photographs.
It licenses its library to companies in the automotive industry and sells licenses for individual images through EvoxStock.com, a site owned by an EVOX affiliate.

“On or about April 10, 2026, a review of EVOX’s server logs revealed that BYTEDANCE had accessed the servers of EvoxStock.com without authorization, and wrongfully copied 7,095 of EVOX’s Images without license,” the EVOX complaint states.

“… BYTEDANCE had accessed the servers of EvoxStock.com without authorization, and wrongfully copied 7,095 of EVOX’s Images without license.”
The images are listed, alongside their copyright registration numbers, in an exhibit to the complaint that runs to around 100 pages.
EVOX claims that ByteDance used the images to train Seedream, which creates pictures in response to text prompts typed in by users.

The lawsuit cites ByteDance’s published material on Seedream 4.0, which it says refers to the use of “HTML-based data retrieval” to build “high-quality editing data pairs.”
“The term ‘HTML-based data retrieval’ appears to reference the online collection of data â although BYTEDANCE is careful not to explain that image data was harvested from online sources without authorization,” EVOX argues.

The complaint goes on to allege that ByteDance “has apparently admitted that it scoured sources from across the internet â including the servers of EvoxStock.com â to build the size of the dataset used to train Seedream.”
The filing includes side-by-side comparisons of EVOX photographs and images it says were generated by Seedream 4.5 from text prompts.
The examples show a 2021 Audi Sportback Premium Plus, a 2021 Audi TT Coupe, and a 2021 Chevrolet Silverado.

EVOX argues that its photos reflect a set of creative choices â including camera height, lighting, a white curved backdrop, and soft shadows beneath each vehicle â that Seedream’s outputs can replicate.
“The propensity of Seedream to duplicate the expressive creative elements of EVOX’s copyrighted Images over and over again is not an accident,” the complaint claims.

“EVOX is informed and believes that Seedream is specifically designed to produce image outputs that can replace the originals that were used to ‘train’ it.”
EVOX says it has invested approximately USD $56 million in its image library over three decades.
“The value of EVOX’s licensing business has justified this investment, and EVOX still generates millions of dollars per year in licensing revenue,” the filing states.

“But Seedream and other image generators now pose an existential threat to EVOX.”
According to the complaint, a license for a single EVOX image can exceed USD $1,300, while ByteDance “can now replicate the same or substantially similar image for a few cents.”
EVOX also goes beyond Seedream’s outputs, arguing that the AI model itself is an unauthorized derivative work built from its photographs.

According to the complaint, Seedream “is built upon and integrates a highly compressed, mathematical copy of the EVOX Images and other copyrighted materials that were used to train it.”
The lawsuit further argues that if ByteDance blames Seedream’s users for any copying, it is still liable for contributory infringement.
The complaint says ByteDance knew or should have known that users would generate copies of EVOX’s images with Seedream, and that it has the ability to stop them.
“BYTEDANCE has made a conscious decision not to prohibit, discourage, or even impede infringement by others,” EVOX alleges.

With 7,095 images listed in the complaint, that framework would put the theoretical maximum at more than USD $1 billion, if each image were counted as a separate work and the infringement were found to be willful.
That first condition is not a given.

The images are registered in groups, with many sharing a single copyright registration number, and the complaint states that each EVOX image has “independent economic value” â a factor courts have weighed when deciding whether works registered together should count separately.
Alternatively, EVOX says it may seek its actual damages and ByteDance’s profits from the alleged infringement.
It is also seeking interest and legal costs.
The complaint does not specify a damages figure and does not specifically ask the court to order ByteDance to stop offering Seedream.
On August 17, ByteDance and the Motion Picture Association (MPA) announced a global agreement setting out intellectual property safeguards for Seedream and ByteDance’s AI video generator, Seedance.
That deal came after the MPA sent ByteDance a cease-and-desist letter in February relating to Seedream 5.0 Lite and Seedance 2.0.

“ByteDance respects the intellectual property rights that underpin creative industries around the world, and we believe responsible innovation in AI goes hand in hand with meaningful protections for rightsholders,” said John Rogovin, ByteDance’s General Counsel, when the agreement was announced.

The EVOX complaint cites the MPA agreement, before adding: “Unfortunately, by using unlicensed copies of EVOX’s copyrighted Images to develop Seedream, BYTEDANCE has exhibited a willingness to disregard the intellectual property rights of smaller copyright owners.”
The ByteDance case is the latest in a series of copyright lawsuits EVOX has filed against AI developers this year.

In July, EVOX sued Stability AI, Runway AI, Hugging Face, and DeviantArt, alleging that links to more than 100,000 of its photographs appeared in a dataset used to train the Stable Diffusion image generator.
EVOX has since filed similar claims against Google and Midjourney, according to Bloomberg Law.
EVOX ‘s argument that an AI model can itself contain copies of its training material is one that music rightsholders have also taken to court.

In November 2025, the Munich Regional Court ruled in favor of German collecting society GEMA in its case against OpenAI, finding that the models behind ChatGPT had stored song lyrics and could reproduce them when prompted by users.
On July 31, the same court ruled against AI music generator Suno in a second GEMA case, which alleged that Suno’s model had stored and reproduced musical works from GEMA’s repertoire.
Suno has said it disagrees with the ruling.
ByteDance, meanwhile, has been developing its own music AI technology, including a suite of music generation models called Seed-Music, as MBW has reported.
